name: MMMU: A Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Expert AGI
description: MMMU is a benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning. It includes 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering. These questions span 30 subjects and 183 subfields, comprising 30 highly heterogeneous image types, such as charts, diagrams, maps, tables, music sheets, and chemical structures.
creator: Xiang Yue, Yuansheng Ni, Kai Zhang, Tianyu Zheng, Ruoqi Liu, Ge Zhang, Samuel Stevens, Dongfu Jiang, Weiming Ren, Yuxuan Sun, Cong Wei, Botao Yu, Ruibin Yuan, Renliang Sun, Ming Yin, Boyuan Zheng, Zhenzhu Yang, Yibo Liu, Wenhao Huang, Huan Sun, Yu Su, Wenhu Chen

MMMU: A Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Expert AGI. arXiv preprint arXiv:2311.16502, 2023.
rai:dataCollection: Data is primarily collected from free online resources, quizzes, textbooks, and other study materials. Over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in 30 different majors assisted in question collection. They collected multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources, creating new questions based on their expertise where necessary. The annotators were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations, avoiding data from sites prohibiting copy and redistribution. Given data contamination concerns, annotators were advised to select questions without immediately available answers, such as those with answers in separate documents or at the end of textbooks.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping, Document analysis
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Questions sourced from college exams, quizzes, textbooks, and online resources across 30 subjects spanning six disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Data quality control was performed in multiple stages. In the first stage, lexical overlap and source URL similarity were employed to identify potential duplicate problems. Suspected duplicates were reviewed by authors to identify and eliminate duplications. The second stage involved distributing problems among co-authors for format and typo checking, ensuring adherence to a standardized format and undertaking necessary corrections. In the third stage, authors categorized problems into four difficulty levels: very easy, easy, medium, and hard. Approximately 10% of problems classified as very easy were excluded from the benchmark.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in 30 different majors assisted in question collection and annotation.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors believe MMMU will prove instrumental in developing next-generation multimodal foundation models and monitoring progress towards Expert AGI. The benchmark is designed to push the boundaries of what large multimodal models can achieve in expert-level understanding and reasoning.
rai:dataLimitations: The manual curation process may carry biases. The focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI. MMMU combines multiple-choice questions with concise open-ended questions to balance complexity and practicality, but this may not capture all aspects of expert-level reasoning. The benchmark may not represent a sufficient test for Expert AGI as there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and '90th percentile of skilled adults,' nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI should tackle.
rai:dataUseCases: MMMU is designed for evaluating multimodal models on college-level multi-discipline tasks. The dataset is divided into a few-shot development set (5 questions per subject), a validation set (approximately 900 questions), and a test set (10.5K questions). The benchmark is intended to measure three essential skills in large multimodal models: perception, knowledge, and reasoning. It is used for testing models' capabilities in expert-level visual perception and deliberate reasoning with subject-specific knowledge.
